1.title: The Summer Everything Changed
paragraphs: When I look back on my childhood, one summer is clearer than all the others. I was ten, and we lived in a small house in Honda, Tolima. Back then, life was simple. I used to wake up early, ride my bike to the river and swim with my cousins until lunch. My grandmother used to make sancocho every Sunday, and the whole street used to smell of it.

Then, one afternoon in July, something happened. My father came home early, which he never did, and sat down at the kitchen table. At the time, I didn't notice anything strange. Suddenly my mother started crying. My father had a new job in Bogotá, and we had to move house in two weeks.
I was angry. I didn't want to leave the river, my friends or my grandmother. I refused to pack my things, and I didn't speak to my father for three days.

That was twenty years ago. Bogotá was cold and grey at first, but I made new friends and later I studied engineering there. I quit my first job last year and now I work for a company that builds bridges — some of them over rivers like the one in Honda. My memories of that summer are still with me, but now I understand my father's decision.

1.title: Interview: The Phone That Saved My Life
paragraphs: Ricardo Salazar, 34, is a designer from Pereira. Five years ago he quit social media. We asked him about it.

What were your habits back then? I used to check my phone two hundred times a day. I used to look at Instagram before I got out of bed, and I didn't use to read books at all. At the time, I thought it was normal.

When did you notice there was a problem? One night in 2021 I was driving home and I looked at a message. Suddenly a motorbike appeared in front of me. I stopped just in time. Nothing happened, but I was shaking. That night I deleted every app.
Was it difficult? Very! For the first week I used to touch my pocket all the time, looking for the phone. But after a month I noticed I was calmer. I slept better, too.
Do you miss anything? I miss some photos from friends, but not much. I've got a basic phone now. I call people instead of sending messages.
How do you look back on that night? It was the best bad memory of my life. I didn't use to have time for anything. Now I read about thirty books a year.

2.title: Shopping List for the Paseo de Olla
paragraphs: Every January, the Torres family goes on a 'paseo de olla' to the river near Melgar. This year cousin Natalia is in charge of the food, and she's messaging her aunt.

Natalia: Hi, Tía Rocío! Could you tell me how many people are coming? I need to know the quantity of food. Rocío: About twenty, I think. A couple of babies, too. Natalia: OK! I wonder whether we have enough pots. Do you know if Uncle Alfonso is bringing his big one? Rocío: Yes, he is. It's huge — there's plenty of room for a sancocho for thirty!

Natalia: Great. How much chicken do we need? Rocío: A lot. Buy six kilos. And a little salt — we always run out of salt. Natalia: Ha! Every year. What about plantains? Rocío: Just a few. Fifteen is enough. Natalia: And cassava? Rocío: A large amount. Everybody loves it.

Natalia: Do you know where I can buy plastic containers? I want to take the food home that we don't eat. Rocío: There's a shop next to the church. And please be polite to Don Eusebio, the owner. He's a bit grumpy!
Natalia: Haha, OK. Can you tell me what time we're leaving? Rocío: Six in the morning. Don't be late!

2.title: Notice: The Community Food Bank Needs You
paragraphs: The Barrio La Esperanza Food Bank helps over a hundred families every month. Right now we have plenty of rice and pasta, but we are running out of other important things. Here is what we need.

We don't have enough cooking oil. Just a couple of bottles from each family would make a big difference. We also have very little milk powder and only a few tins of tuna. We need a large amount of lentils and beans, because they are cheap and healthy.
Please don't bring fresh food like meat or fish. We have no fridge, and we can't keep it safe. Fruit and vegetables are OK if you bring them on Saturday morning.

Many people ask us: 'Could you tell me where the food bank is?' We are in the community hall, next to the football field. Others wonder whether they can volunteer. Yes, you can! We need a few people to help on Saturdays. You only need a couple of hours and a smile.
Please bring the food in a closed container or a strong bag. And remember: every quantity helps, from a kilo of rice to a whole box.
If you'd like to know what time we open, it's 8 a.m. to 12 p.m. Thank you for being such a generous neighbourhood!

3.title: Small Flat, Big City
paragraphs: Six months ago, I moved from my parents' house in Sogamoso to a tiny studio apartment in Chapinero, Bogotá. People ask me if it was a good decision. The honest answer is: yes and no.

Let's start with the good things. The location is extremely convenient. I can walk to work in fifteen minutes, so I don't have to put up with TransMilenio at rush hour, which is always too crowded. There are more cafés and bookshops on my street than in my whole town.

Now the drawbacks. First, space. My flat isn't big enough for a sofa AND a desk, so I settled for a desk. There's just about enough room for my bed and a small table. Second, the noise: there's a bar downstairs, and on Fridays it's impossible to sleep before 2 a.m. Third, the expense. Rent is a lot higher than I expected — it takes almost half my salary.
Sometimes I complain to my friends, but they say I'm lucky. Their flats are further from work and not as nice as mine.
Do I have any wishes? Of course. I wish my flat had a balcony. I wish the bar closed earlier. And I wish I could cook something decent in my tiny kitchen! But for now, it's home, and I'm happy.

4.title: Bucket List: What I've Done So Far
paragraphs: When I turned thirty, I wrote a list of twenty things I wanted to do before forty. I'm thirty-five now, so it's time to check my progress. So far, I've achieved eleven of them.

Some steps were easy. I've already learned to swim — I took lessons at a public pool in 2022, after many years of fear. I've also visited San Andrés, and I've seen the 'sea of seven colours'. It was the most beautiful experience of my life.

Other things took longer. For years I wanted to run a half marathon. First, I joined a running club. Then I ran five kilometres, after that ten, and finally, last July, I finished the Bogotá half marathon in two hours and twelve minutes. I cried at the finish line!

But there are things I haven't done yet. I haven't learned to play the guitar — I bought one in 2021, but I never got round to taking lessons. I haven't climbed Nevado del Ruiz yet, either. And I haven't written my novel. I've had the idea since I was a student, but up to now I've only written two chapters.
Recently I looked up a writing course online. It starts next month. Maybe forty-year-old me will be a writer after all!

4.title: How Rosa Built Her Bakery
paragraphs: Rosa Mosquera has run 'Pan del Pacífico', a small bakery in Quibdó, since 2019. Up to now, it has sold more than half a million pandebonos. But the road to success wasn't easy.

Rosa grew up in a family of cooks. First, she worked in her aunt's restaurant for five years. Then, in 2017, she lost her job when the restaurant closed. 'That was the hardest moment,' she says. 'But it was also the beginning.'

After that, she looked up recipes online every night and baked bread in her mother's small oven. Next, she started selling it to her neighbours. Soon people were waiting outside her door at six in the morning. Finally, with a small loan from a women's cooperative, she opened her shop.
So far, Rosa has employed seven people — all of them young mothers from her neighbourhood. She has recently opened a second shop near the river, and she has already trained two new bakers.
Has she achieved her dream yet? 'Not yet,' she smiles. 'I want to teach a baking class for teenagers. I haven't got round to it because I'm always busy, but it's the next step.'
Rosa's experience shows that one bad moment can be the start of something great.

5.title: Rainy Season Warning for Travellers
paragraphs: The national weather service, IDEAM, has warned that the rainy season will be stronger than usual this year. Heavy rain is likely to start in the second week of October and it will probably continue until early December.

What does this mean for travellers? Roads in the mountains are likely to close because of landslides, especially between Bogotá and Villavicencio. 'If you're planning a road trip, you'd better check the road conditions before you leave,' says Andrea Bernal, who is in charge of road safety for the region. 'And you should always have a backup plan.'

Airlines are going to change some flight times, too. Passengers will need to arrive at the airport earlier, and some flights may be postponed. 'It's not urgent to cancel your trip,' Bernal explains, 'but you ought to buy travel insurance.'
Some hotels already require guests to confirm their reservations a week before they arrive. Others are going to offer free changes of date.

Experts say that the weather is changing every year. 'We'll see more extreme seasons in the future,' says climate scientist Dr. Pablo Henao. 'Many families end up losing their homes to floods. The government has to prepare better.'
The next official report is about to come out on Friday.

Sofía: Great. I think we should meet on Sunday to practise. The professor requires everyone to speak for three minutes. Laura: Good idea. We'd better meet early, because I'm likely to be tired after my cousin's wedding on Saturday night!

paragraphs: Hi Julián, welcome to the flat! We're really happy that you're here. Before you settle in, here are a few things we'd like to ask you. Don't worry, we're not very strict!

Second, could you put away your dishes after you eat? Our kitchen is small, and it fills up quickly. If you see dishes in the sink, could you wash them? We'll do the same for you.

6.title: Ask the Boss: How Do I Say No?
paragraphs: Dear Mónica, I started working at a call centre in Barranquilla three months ago. My colleagues always ask me for favours. 'Would you mind covering my shift?' 'Could you pick up my lunch?' 'Can you fill in this report for me?' I always say yes, and now I'm exhausted. How can I say no politely? — Sebastián
Dear Sebastián, this is a very common problem, especially for new employees. You want people to like you, so you say yes to everything. But you have to look after yourself, too.
First, you don't need to answer right away. Say: 'Let me check my schedule and I'll get back to you.' This gives you time to think.
Second, learn to say 'I'm afraid I can't.' It's polite and clear. For example: 'I'm afraid I can't cover your shift on Saturday. I have plans with my family.' You don't need a long explanation.
Third, offer a smaller favour. 'I can't fill out the whole report, but I'll help you with the first part.'
Finally, if a colleague keeps asking, talk to your supervisor. They can sort out the problem before it gets worse.
Remember: when you say no to some things, your yes becomes more valuable. Good luck! — Mónica

7.title: Five Gadgets Every Traveller Needs
paragraphs: Travelling around Colombia is amazing, but it can be hard on your things. Here are five small devices that really come in handy.
1. A power bank. It's used for charging your phone when there's no electricity. On long bus trips, it's worth taking one with at least 10,000 mAh. Make sure to charge it the night before.
2. A dry bag. The point of this bag is to keep your phone and documents dry. You'll need it in order to visit places like Caño Cristales or La Guajira's beaches, where water is everywhere.
3. A headlamp. This little tool is perfect for walking at night in small towns where the streets are dark. It's also used to read in hostels without waking up other guests.
4. A water filter bottle. Its purpose is to clean tap water, so you can avoid buying plastic bottles. Follow the instructions carefully and change the filter every two months.
5. A universal adapter. Colombia uses American plugs, but if you travel on to other countries, you'll need one to keep using your devices.
Final tip: don't take expensive gadgets you don't need. Try to travel light, and remember to keep your important things in your hand luggage.

7.title: How to Make the Perfect Tinto
paragraphs: Ask ten Colombians how to make tinto and you'll get ten different answers. Here are the instructions my grandfather in Huila taught me. They're worth following!
First, choose your coffee. Try to buy it from a small farm, not a supermarket. Freshly ground coffee is best, so keep the beans in a closed container and grind them only before using them.
You'll need a pot, water, coffee and a cloth filter called a 'colador'. This simple tool is used for straining the coffee. The point of a cloth filter is to keep the flavour strong but clean.

Heat the water until it's almost boiling, but avoid letting it boil for long, because that burns the coffee. Then add two spoons of coffee for every cup of water. Stir it, turn off the heat and wait three minutes in order to let the flavour develop.
Next, pour it slowly through the colador. Make sure you don't squeeze the cloth — the coffee becomes bitter. If you like it sweet, add panela, not sugar. That's the traditional way.
Finally, remember to wash the colador with only water, never soap. Keep using the same one for months; old coladores make the best coffee.
A good tinto comes in handy on cold mornings in Bogotá — or any morning, really!

8.title: The Day I Became a Teacher
paragraphs: I remember the moment when I decided to become a teacher. It was 2015, and I was studying business administration at a university in Tunja. I didn't really like my classes, but I didn't know what else to do.

That year I started volunteering on Saturdays in a small school in a village near Villa de Leyva. I used to help the children with their reading while their teacher prepared lunch. One morning, a shy boy called Kevin read a whole page for the first time. As soon as he finished, he looked at me and smiled. That was my turning point.
After I got home, I called my mother. 'I want to change my degree,' I said. She was quiet for a long time. Meanwhile, I was very nervous. Eventually, she said, 'If that makes you happy, do it.'

Changing wasn't easy. I had to start again in the education faculty, and in the meantime I worked in a bakery to pay for my studies. While my friends were finishing their degrees, I was in my second year.
By the time I graduated in 2021, I was twenty-seven. I realised that age wasn't important. Now I teach in a rural school in Boyacá. I'll stay there until I retire — or until my students stop smiling!

8.title: A Short History of the Chiva Bus
paragraphs: If you've ever visited a Colombian village, you've probably seen a chiva: a colourful wooden bus with open sides. But do you know its history?

The first chivas appeared in the 1910s and 1920s, a period when Colombia had very few roads and almost no trains in the countryside. Before chivas arrived, farmers carried their products on mules, and a trip to the market could take two or three days.

When local mechanics began building wooden bodies on top of truck engines, everything changed. The chiva could carry people, animals and sacks of coffee at the same time. While passengers sat on wooden benches, the cargo travelled on the roof.

Over time, chivas became symbols of popular art. Artists painted them with flowers, landscapes and the names of saints. Meanwhile, cities grew and modern buses arrived. Eventually, chivas almost disappeared from the big cities.

Today they have a new life. In Medellín, Cartagena and Bogotá, 'chivas rumberas' carry tourists who dance while the bus drives around the city at night. In the meantime, in rural areas, many chivas still do their original job.
By the time you finish reading this, a chiva somewhere in the Andes is probably climbing a mountain road, full of people, music and bananas.

9.title: Medellín: Then, Now and Next
paragraphs: Thirty years ago, few tourists visited Medellín. Back then, the city had a bad reputation, and many neighbourhoods on the hills were isolated from the centre. What did it use to be like for the people there? 'It used to take me two hours to get to work,' remembers Doña Luz, who lives in Santo Domingo Savio. 'There were no good roads, only steep stairs.'

Nowadays the situation is very different. In 2004 the city opened its first Metrocable line, a cable car connected to the metro. Today Doña Luz gets to the centre in thirty minutes. Libraries, parks and outdoor escalators have gradually changed the life of many communities. One consequence is tourism: thousands of visitors now come to see Comuna 13 every week.

But what will happen next? Experts expect the city to keep growing, and that brings new problems. If the population continues to rise, traffic and pollution will get worse. Unless the city builds more public transport, people will end up spending hours in their cars again.

There is also a new trend: rents are going up in popular areas because of short-term rentals for tourists. 'Tourism is good, as long as local families can stay in their homes,' says urban planner Camilo Restrepo. 'In case prices keep rising, the city will need new rules.'
The future is open, but one thing is clear: Medellín has learned that it can improve.

9.title: What Will You Do If It Rains?
paragraphs: I've been a tour guide in Bogotá for ten years, and tourists always ask me the same question: 'What will we do if it rains?' My answer: 'If it rains, we'll get wet — and we'll have fun!'

Seriously, though, the weather here has changed a lot. Back then, when I started, we used to have two clear rainy seasons. Nowadays it can rain any month, any day, at any hour. Climate experts say this trend will continue, so I've gradually changed how I work.

First, I always carry extra umbrellas in case someone forgets theirs. Second, I've created indoor options. If the rain is heavy, we'll visit the Gold Museum instead of walking around La Candelaria. If it stops, we'll go up to Monserrate.

My advice for visitors: you'll enjoy Bogotá as long as you bring a jacket. Don't expect sunny weather all day. The morning might be beautiful, but you'll end up needing a raincoat by three o'clock. Unless you check the forecast, you might get a surprise.

One consequence of all this rain is a positive one: the mountains around the city are incredibly green. And when the sun finally comes out, Bogotá is one of the most beautiful cities in the world. If you come, you won't regret it!

10.title: Why I Gave Up My Car
paragraphs: Two years ago I sold my car. My friends thought I was crazy. 'How will you get to work?' they asked. By bike, of course. Here's why.

First, I couldn't stand sitting in traffic. Driving from Usaquén to my office took more than an hour every morning, and I was always fed up with the noise and the stress. Now I cycle on the ciclorrutas and it takes forty minutes. I really enjoy riding through the parks in the morning.
Second, money. Because of petrol, parking and insurance, my car cost me almost a million pesos a month. That's a good reason to change, isn't it?

Some people say, 'I don't mind cycling, but I hate getting wet.' So do I! But I bought a good raincoat, and it was worth it. Others say, 'I prefer taking a taxi because it's safer.' That's true in some areas, so I always choose well-lit roads.
I'm not into extreme sports, and I'm not a super athlete. I'm forty-five and a bit overweight — or I was! I've lost eight kilos since I started.
My wife doesn't like cycling. 'Neither do I in the rain,' I tell her. But she agrees that I'm happier. Being bored in a car isn't a life. If you can, try it for one week. You might never go back.

10.title: Our Readers Answer: Beach or Mountains?
paragraphs: This month we asked our readers a simple question: 'Do you prefer going to the beach or to the mountains for your holidays?' Here are some of their answers.

Natalia, 28, Cali: 'The beach, definitely! I'm really into diving, and I enjoy lying in the sun with a good book. I can't stand cold weather because I grew up in a hot city. My favourite place is Bahía Solano.'

Jorge, 52, Pasto: 'I prefer the mountains. The beach is too hot for me and I don't like sand in my clothes. My wife doesn't either! We love hiking in Nariño. Walking up to the Laguna de la Cocha is worth it — the views are incredible.'
Camila, 19, Barranquilla: 'I live next to the sea, so going to the beach on holiday is boring for me. I'm fed up with hot weather! I'd love to see snow in the Nevado del Ruiz one day.'

Andrés, 35, Bogotá: 'I don't mind either. The important thing for me is the company. If I'm with my friends, I'm never bored. But because of my job, I can only travel in December, so I usually go where the flights are cheaper.'
Results: 54% of readers chose the beach and 46% chose the mountains. The main reason? The weather!

11.title: The Story of the Arepa Machine
paragraphs: Arepas are eaten by millions of Colombians every day. But how are they produced in such large quantities? Much of the answer is a machine that was invented in a small workshop in Medellín.

Originally, arepas were made by hand. Women ground the corn, shaped the dough with their palms and cooked it on a clay plate. It was hard work, and only a few dozen arepas could be prepared in an hour.

In the 1960s, a mechanic named Gustavo Arango (a fictional name for this story) was asked by a local restaurant to build something faster. His first machine was built from old car parts. It was based on a simple idea: two rollers flatten the dough, and a metal circle cuts it.

Today, machines like his are produced in factories and sold all over Latin America. In a typical arepa company, the corn is cooked, ground and shaped automatically. Quality checks are carried out every hour, and only trained workers are allowed to handle the machines.
Every morning, thousands of packets are delivered to supermarkets and corner shops. Some boxes are damaged on the way, but most arrive in perfect condition.
Of course, many families still prefer the homemade kind. As one grandmother told us: 'Machines are fast, but love is not required by a machine.'

11.title: What Happened to My Package?
paragraphs: Dear Customer Service, I am writing about an order that I made on your website on 3 May (order number 48219). It was delivered yesterday, but I am not happy with the way it was handled.

First, the package was left outside my building, not given to the doorman as I requested. It was raining, so the box was completely wet. Second, when I opened it, I found that the lamp inside was damaged. The glass was broken into three pieces.

According to your website, all products are packed carefully and checked before they are sent. However, there was no protective material in the box. It seems that the lamp was simply put inside without any paper or plastic.
I contacted your agent by chat, and I was told to send photos. I sent them, but I have not received an answer in four days.

Your return policy says that customers are allowed to return damaged products within thirty days. I would like a new lamp to be sent to me, or a full refund. I also hope this information is passed to the delivery company, so that the problem is not repeated.
I have been a customer since 2020, and until now I have always been happy with your service. I look forward to your reply.
Yours faithfully, Carolina Vélez

12.title: A Very Long Night at the Hospital
paragraphs: Last Saturday I was watching a movie with my roommate when my phone rang. It was my sister Juliana. 'Dad's in the hospital,' she said. 'He was cutting wood in the garden and he hurt his hand.'
I got a taxi right away. While I was travelling to the hospital, I was thinking about my father. He's been working in the garden all day every weekend lately, and he never uses gloves.
When I arrived, Juliana was sitting in the waiting room. She looked exhausted. 'I've been waiting here for three hours,' she said. 'The doctors are dealing with an emergency.'
We were talking about what to do when, just then, I ran into an old friend from school, Daniel. He's a nurse now! He said he would look into it. Twenty minutes later, a doctor came to see my father.

The cut wasn't serious, but my father needed six stitches. While the doctor was working, my dad kept making jokes. 'I've been planning to take a holiday,' he said, 'but this isn't what I had in mind!'
We got home at 3 a.m. Since then, Juliana and I have been keeping an eye on him. He's been making good progress, and he promises he'll wear gloves from now on.

12.title: Progress Report: The Community Garden
paragraphs: To: Members of the Junta de Acción Comunal, Barrio San Martín. From: Diana Ortiz, garden coordinator.
We have been working on the community garden since February, and I would like to update you on our progress.

What we have done: Fifteen volunteers have been coming every Saturday morning. We have been growing tomatoes, lettuce, coriander and beans. Lately, we have also been teaching children from the local school how to plant seeds. They have been really enthusiastic!

Problems: In April, while we were preparing the soil, we discovered that part of the land was full of rubbish. We spent two weekends dealing with it. Then, in May, while the plants were growing, someone stole our water hose. Recently, we have been keeping an eye on the garden at night, and nothing else has disappeared.
Next steps: The city council is looking into our request for a small storage room. We have been asking for it since March, but the process is slow. Meanwhile, the tools are staying in my house!

Finally, I want to thank everyone. Many of us are exhausted after long weeks at work, but we keep coming. The garden is going to give us its first harvest in July, and everyone is invited to the celebration.

13.title: Museum Review: A Fascinating Afternoon
paragraphs: Last Sunday I visited the Museo del Oro in Bogotá with my nephew, who is twelve. I expected him to be bored, but the visit was fascinating for both of us.

The museum, which has more than 30,000 gold objects, is one of the most impressive in Latin America. The pieces that impressed us most were the tiny animals made by the Muisca and Quimbaya people. My nephew was fascinated by a small gold frog whose eyes seemed to follow him around the room.

Not everything was perfect, though. The signs in some rooms were confusing, and we got a little lost on the second floor. The audio guide, which cost 10,000 pesos, was disappointing — it was broken after twenty minutes, and the woman who was in charge of the desk didn't have another one.

The famous 'Offering Room' was the highlight. You enter a dark room, and suddenly the lights come on and you're surrounded by gold. My nephew, who usually comes across as a cool teenager, said 'Wow!' out loud.
After three hours of walking, we were exhausted. It's an exhausting visit if you try to see everything, so take breaks. The café, which is on the ground floor, is reliable and not too expensive.
Overall: highly recommended. The only annoying thing was the crowd at the entrance. Go early!

13.title: Meet the Team: Our New Volunteers
paragraphs: Every year, our foundation in Cartagena welcomes volunteers who help children with homework and sports. Here are three of the people who joined us this semester.

Ana Lucía, 24, is a psychology student whose dream is to work with teenagers. She comes across as quiet, but she has an impressive talent for listening. 'The first week was exhausting,' she admits, 'but I'm never bored here. The kids are fascinating.'

Tom, 31, is a nurse from Canada who is spending six months in Colombia. He's in charge of the first-aid workshop. At first, he was confused by the coastal accent. 'People speak so fast!' he laughs. 'But now I understand most things.' Tom is very reliable — he has never missed a day.

Don Hernando, 67, is a retired football coach whose team won a regional championship in 1989. He trains the under-12 team, which practises on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The kids find him funny, although some think his whistle is a bit annoying!

Of course, it isn't always easy. Last month, the bus that takes the children home was broken for a week, and it was disappointing to cancel the matches. But the volunteers found a solution: they walked every child home.
Would you like to join a team that makes a difference? Write to us!

14.title: Rules for Visiting the Tayrona Park
paragraphs: Welcome to the Tayrona National Natural Park. This is a protected area and an important sacred place for the Indigenous peoples of the Sierra Nevada. Please read these rules carefully.
Before you enter: All visitors are supposed to buy a ticket and show an ID. Your bags may be checked at the entrance. Plastic bags are strictly prohibited, and alcohol is forbidden inside the park.

Inside the park: You are allowed to swim only on beaches with a green flag, such as La Piscina and Cabo San Juan. On other beaches the currents are extremely strong, and swimmers have died there. You must not feed the animals or take plants, shells or stones with you. Camping is only allowed in official areas.

Please don't assume that the park is open all year. It closes for about a month every year so that nature can recover and the Indigenous communities can carry out spiritual ceremonies. The dates may change, so check the official website before your trip.
If you see evidence of fire, rubbish or illegal fishing, it's your obligation to tell a park ranger. You can figure out where the rangers are by looking for the green uniforms.
Remember: it's unlikely you'll see everything in one day. Perhaps you'll come back! Thank you for protecting this place.

14.title: The Mystery of the Missing Cake
paragraphs: It was Mrs. Patiño's sixtieth birthday, and her family had prepared a surprise party. The cake — a beautiful tres leches — was in the fridge. But when her daughter Paula opened the fridge at six o'clock, it wasn't there.

'Someone must have taken it,' Paula said. 'It can't have disappeared by itself.' Her brother Felipe looked around. 'Perhaps the dog ate it?' 'Impossible,' said Paula. 'The dog isn't allowed in the kitchen, and the fridge door was closed.'
They looked for evidence. There were small white footprints on the floor. 'Those must be from cream,' said Felipe. 'And they're small — it might be one of the kids.'
Paula assumed it was their nephew, Samuel, who is seven and loves sweets. But Samuel was probably innocent — he had been at football practice all afternoon. 'It's unlikely it was him,' she admitted.

Then they figured it out. The footprints led to the garden, where their cousin's twin girls were sitting under a tree, with cream all over their faces — and the cake, almost complete, on a plate between them. 'We were supposed to keep it safe,' said one twin. 'It was a secret mission!'
Everyone laughed. The party went on, the cake was a bit smaller, and Mrs. Patiño said it was the best birthday ever.

15.title: If I Could Go Back…
paragraphs: My grandmother always says, 'Regrets are lessons you didn't want to learn.' This week I asked my followers a hypothetical question: 'If you could change one decision in your life, what would it be?' Here are some of the best answers.

'In hindsight, I should have studied something practical,' wrote Daniela, 29. 'I studied philosophy because I loved it, but I couldn't find a job for two years. If I were eighteen again, I would study nursing and read philosophy in my free time.'
'I turned down a job in Australia when I was 25,' said Jorge, 41. 'My girlfriend didn't want to go, so I stayed. We broke up a year later! I would have had a completely different life.'
'I shouldn't have bought a car on credit,' admitted Luisa, 33. 'Everyone warned me, but I didn't listen. Otherwise, I would have saved enough money for a house by now.'

Not everyone had regrets, though. 'If I were in your shoes, I wouldn't blame myself for anything,' wrote Pedro, 60. 'Every mistake taught me something. Instead of looking back, I prefer looking forward.'
And me? If I had more courage, I would learn to sing in public. Maybe it's worth it to try. What about you?

15.title: Advice Column: I Said No to My Dream Job
paragraphs: Dear Carmen, Last month I was offered a job at a big tech company in Bogotá. The salary was double what I earn now. But I turned it down because I didn't want to leave my parents alone in Popayán. Now I can't stop thinking about it. Should I have accepted? What would you do in my shoes? — Sergio
Dear Sergio, Thank you for your honest letter. First of all, don't blame yourself. You made a decision based on love, and that is never a mistake.

Of course, it's natural to think about hypothetical lives. If you had accepted, you would have more money — but you would also worry about your parents every day. Would that have been worth it? Only you know.
In my experience, regret usually comes from decisions we make because of fear, not because of our values. You weren't afraid; you were caring for your family.

Here is my practical advice. Instead of looking back, look for options. Many tech companies allow remote work now. If I were you, I would write to that company and ask if they have remote positions. Otherwise, look for other companies that do.
And one more lesson: next time, talk to your parents before you decide. They might want you to take the opportunity!
Warm wishes, Carmen

16.title: What the Neighbours Said
paragraphs: Last night there was a meeting in our building to talk about the new rules for the swimming pool. I couldn't go, so my roommate Valentina told me everything this morning.

Apparently, the administrator, Mr. Quintero, said that the pool would close at nine instead of ten. Mrs. Gómez from the fourth floor complained that the children made too much noise in the evenings. Mr. Quintero promised that he would put up new signs.

Then Don Arturo, who is eighty, insisted that the water was too cold. He said he hadn't swum for a month! Somebody pointed out that the heater had been broken since June. The administrator admitted that he had forgotten to call the technician. In other words, nobody had done anything!
Valentina mentioned that a young couple refused to pay the new pool fee. They said they never used the pool. Mr. Quintero told them to send a written letter to the council.
At the end, he asked everyone to respect the new rules and reminded us to bring our residents' cards. He also told the teenagers not to play loud music.
'So, what did they say about our bikes in the garage?' I asked. Valentina laughed. 'Nobody mentioned the bikes. I told you it was a pool meeting!'

16.title: Notes from the Class Meeting
paragraphs: Class 10B — Meeting with the director about the end-of-year trip. Notes taken by Daniel Rojas, class representative.

The director, Mrs. Castaño, told us that the school had approved the trip to the Coffee Region. She said we would visit Salento, the Cocora Valley and a coffee farm. However, she pointed out that the bus company had raised its prices by 15%.

Several students complained that the trip was getting too expensive. Laura mentioned that some families couldn't pay the full amount. Mrs. Castaño admitted that it was a problem and promised to look for a cheaper bus.
Kevin asked if we could stay an extra night. The director refused. She said that the insurance only covered three days. In other words, the plan won't change.
Mrs. Castaño reminded everyone to bring the permission forms by Friday. She also told us not to forget our ID cards and insisted that we must wear the school uniform on the bus.
Apparently, the teacher in charge, Mr. Lozano, said that phones would be allowed only in the evenings. Some students were not happy, but most agreed.
Finally, the director asked us to organise a bake sale to raise money for students who need help. We said we would do it next Thursday.
